reference_title: EM 1110-2-2107, Design of Hydraulic Steel Structures (USACE, dated 1 August 2022)

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Connection design principles (force transfer, ductility/rotation capacity, stress concentration/eccentricity/splice/fixity/fatigue considerations, constraint minimization); welding-code selection (AWS D1.5(M) for cyclic/FCM HSS, AWS D1.1(M) permitted only for redundant non-cyclic HSS); weld-metal selection (undermatching considered for high-strength steel); Fracture Critical Weld (FCW) identification; and bolting requirements (fully tensioned high-strength bolts required, slip-critical connection rules, faying-surface preparation classes, allowed bolt grades, plain/galvanized/stainless bolt coating tradeoffs, bearing/pretensioned/slip-critical/fitted connection types).
sections.body: All connections must be detailed by the Engineer; any deviation from originally specified details must be reviewed/approved by the Engineer. Connections must transfer required forces from structural analysis while maintaining sufficient ductility/rotation capacity, considering stress concentrations, eccentricities, field splices, imposed restraints (fixity), and fatigue resistance. Constraint should be minimized (copes to avoid intersecting welds, weld sizes limited to what satisfies the limit states, avoiding stiff/constrained connections at intersecting members), with environmental/economic/accessibility factors considered especially for field connections. Splices should be avoided where possible, located in low/moderate-stress uncongested areas when required, shown on drawings, with optional fabricator/erector-proposed splices requiring Engineer review/approval. Connections carrying tensile stress should generally use fatigue-resistant detailing even absent fatigue loading, to minimize stress concentration and corrosion-induced fatigue risk. Most HSS use welded connections (avoid intersecting/overlapping/intermittent welds; remove backing bars from CJP welds and grind flush; NDT per Chapter 8). Cyclically loaded members and FCM must use AWS D1.5(M) (recommended for ALL HSS fabrication); AWS D1.1(M) may be used only on redundant, non-cyclically-loaded HSS where fatigue/fracture are not design considerations (connections.welding_code_selection). Weld metal is selected for toughness/strength/base-metal compatibility; undermatching weld strength may be considered for high-strength steel to limit residual stresses. All welds to FCM are considered fracture critical; the Engineer identifies FCM on contract drawings and Fracture Critical Welds (FCW) in shop drawings. Bolting: fully tensioned high-strength bolts are REQUIRED for all HSS structural applications; priming faying surfaces is recommended for corrosion protection (note vinyl primer alone does not qualify as a slip-critical faying surface, and vinyl topcoat does not adhere to inorganic zinc primer). Slip-critical connections are required where slip would inhibit operability and for cyclically loaded HSS -- and are REQUIRED (not merely recommended) for: connections subject to fatigue or load-reversal cycling; connections with oversized holes; connections with slotted holes except where the applied load is approximately normal (80-100 degrees) to the slot's long dimension; and connections where faying-surface slip would harm structural performance. Faying surfaces must be prepared per RCSC S348/AISC 360 (abrasive techniques or slip-resistant coatings); clean mill scale qualifies as Class A, blast-cleaned steel as Class B (connections.faying_surface_class -- this manual gives no numeric slip coefficient for either class, see AISC 360/RCSC S348 directly). Bolts must be proportioned for the external load PLUS prying-action tension from deformation of connected parts. Only ASTM F3125 Grade A325, ASTM F3125 Grade A490, or ASTM F3148 bolts (with compatible nuts/washers) are permitted for structural connections; ASTM A307 or SAE J429 Grade 5/8 bolts are for non-structural applications only (connections.bolt_grade_check). Plain (uncoated) bolts corrode in submerged environments and should be painted/coated after assembly. Galvanized bolts (hot-dipped or mechanically galvanized) cannot be interchanged between types; some high-strength bolts (e.g. ASTM F3125 Grade A490) cannot be galvanized due to hydrogen embrittlement risk; unpainted galvanized bolts are not recommended for normally-submerged conditions (rapid zinc sacrifice) but may suit infrequently-submerged or accessible noncritical locations (seals, fenders). Stainless steel bolts, while corrosion-resistant, risk galvanic corrosion with carbon-steel HSS in submerged conditions and are generally not recommended with plain-carbon-steel structures; both stainless and plain-carbon bolts tend to freeze in place over time in submerged service and require cutting to remove. Painted galvanized bolts are generally recommended for most HSS connections. Bearing connections (snug-tightened or fully pretensioned) transfer shear via bolt-to-plate bearing; design limit states are bolt shear and connected-material bearing strength; bearing connections must NOT be used where fatigue/cyclic loads apply. Fully pretensioned connections are required for ALL structural connections (those transmitting primary live/dead load); pretensioning reduces movement under dynamic/vibration loading and transmits shear/tension via bolt bearing, so faying surfaces need no special preparation for load transfer (though soft coatings like vinyl paint or gaskets may prevent achieving pretension); faying surfaces are still prepared per UFGS 09 97 02 for coating-system reasons. Slip-critical connections transfer shear (or shear+tension) via clamping-force friction between prepared faying surfaces, without displacement, and require BOTH proper surface preparation AND proper bolt pretensioning. Fitted bolts (also called Body Fit, Turned, or Match Drilled Bolts) are used in existing structures to create slip-critical-equivalent or movement-sensitive connections via reamed/turned-to-fit holes/bolts (clearances from hundredths to thousandths of an inch, termed Force/Press/Freeze Fit, symbolized LN/FN); unlike friction-based slip-critical connections, fitted connections ensure equal shear distribution across all bolts on load application, but AISC gives no code guidance for their design -- clearance must be determined case-by-case, with ASTM A449 bar stock (material-equivalent to F3125 A325) recommended for new fitted connections, and consultation with an experienced (typically mechanical) bolting engineer recommended.
key_points: AWS D1.5(M) for cyclic/FCM HSS (recommended for all HSS); AWS D1.1(M) only for redundant non-cyclic HSS
Structural bolts: ASTM F3125 A325/A490 or F3148 only; A307/SAE J429 Gr5/Gr8 are non-structural only
Fully tensioned/pretensioned bolts REQUIRED for all HSS structural connections; slip-critical required for fatigue/oversized-hole/slotted-hole/slip-sensitive cases
Faying surface classes: clean mill scale = Class A, blast-cleaned = Class B (no numeric slip coefficient printed -- see AISC 360/RCSC S348)
Bearing connections prohibited where fatigue/cyclic loads apply
Vinyl primer alone does NOT qualify as a slip-critical faying surface
No AISC code guidance exists for fitted-bolt connection design
sections.applicability: Selecting the connection type (bearing/pretensioned/slip-critical/fitted), bolt grade, and welding code appropriate to a given HSS connection's loading and criticality.

sections.title: Detailing for Performance
sections.summary: Detailing to minimize residual stress/restraint/constraint (weld sequencing, inspection requirements, stress relieving for large/thick/highly-restrained weldments), fatigue-resistant detailing (Chapter 5), fracture-resistant detailing (avoiding restraint/constraint), and corrosion-control detailing (drainage, seal welds, adequate access for weld wrapping).
sections.body: The Engineer should design HSS and details to minimize residual stress, restraint, and constraint; fabrication requirements (weld sequence, inspection) must be specified for thick-plate or highly-constrained weldments with large tensile residual stresses, and stress relieving considered for large weldments, thick-plate girders, and high restraint. Fatigue-resistant details per Chapter 5 must be selected for all cyclically loaded HSS (including vibration/high-cycle fatigue) to minimize crack initiation/propagation. Fracture-resistant details avoiding restraint/constraint must be selected for all HSS to reduce cracking potential. Corrosion-control detailing provides sufficient drainage and sealing of all connections: properly sized/located drain holes; minimum-size seal welds per AISC/AWS; sufficient room (copes, access holes) to accommodate weld wrapping; in non-submerged/low-moisture conditions welds may terminate short of copes, and bolted connections should use fully pretensioned bolts with enough bolts to exclude moisture.
key_points: Stress relieving considered for large/thick/highly-restrained weldments
Corrosion-control detailing: drain holes, seal welds, weld-wrap access, moisture-excluding bolt patterns
sections.applicability: Detailing checklist for in-service performance (fatigue/fracture/corrosion resistance).

sections.title: Detailing for Fabrication
sections.summary: Detailing to accommodate fabrication processes: individual-member fabrication before final assembly, adequate access for welding/blasting/painting/inspection, distortion control via weld sequencing (fabricator-developed, Engineer-reviewed plan; mockups for complex/critical components), adequate support/restraint during fabrication (spread, not concentrated, residual stress), access for NDT, and bolting-access provisions.
sections.body: All HSS must be detailed to accommodate fabrication processes. Individual members should be fabricated before final assembly; sufficient access is needed for welding, sandblasting, painting/coatings, and inspection equipment/provisions (access hatches, safety railing) for frequently inspected areas. Weld sequencing controls residual stress during fabrication (e.g. completing CJP welds in girder flanges before assembling pieces into the final structure); before fabrication, the fabricator develops (and the Engineer reviews) a weld sequencing plan, with a mockup specified for complex/critical components. An adequate amount of support/restraint should be provided during fabrication to keep members straight, without over-restraining (which introduces large LOCALIZED residual stresses) -- restraint should spread residual stresses globally rather than concentrate them. Access for NDT should be considered during design/shop-drawing development. Bolted connections need sufficient access for bolt installation and tightening.
key_points: Fabricator develops, Engineer reviews, the weld sequencing plan; mockups for complex/critical components
Support/restraint during fabrication should SPREAD residual stress, not concentrate it locally
NDT and bolt-tightening access must be planned into the detailing, not left to fabrication improvisation
sections.applicability: Detailing checklist for fabrication quality and constructability.
